guard.title: The Crystal Palace dinosaurs, London’s Victorian vision of prehistoric Britain
guard.text: Rory Walsh explores South London’s Victorian vision of prehistoric Britain. The 30 or so statues, built just after Bleak House was published, were the world’s first life-sized models of extinct animals. When they were unveiled to the public in 1855, the dinosaurs were a sensation, intended to educate Victorian visitors about the emerging science of palaeontology. The statues were placed in a carefully landscaped Geological Court. Winding footpaths still lead around three scenic islands set within a tidal lake. The islands represent scenes from the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, with the statues chronologically arranged to create a walk through Deep Time. Alongside them, a set of Geological Illustrations showcases Britain’s geological and mineral resources. stands proudly on display after Britain’s driest summer.

guard.title: LGBTQ+ refugees face persecution in South Sudan’s Gorom settlement
guard.text: By Kate Plummer. Gorom Refugee Settlement lies 26 kilometres southwest of Juba, South Sudan’s capital. The camp, built in 2010, is under the authority of the South Sudanese government through its Commission for Refugee Affairs and is supported by several organisations, including UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, the Red Cross and Peace Winds. It was originally intended to house 2,500 refugees fleeing conflict in Ethiopia, but it is now overflowing. According to a UNHCR spokesperson, some 16,000 refugees live in the settlement and on 22 June this year, the camp stopped registering new arrivals. Image: Kate Plummer.

guard.title: As yellow-eyed penguins disappear, conservationists focus on deaths in fishing nets
guard.text: OTAGO PENINSULA, Aotearoa New Zealand — Sandfly Bay was long a key nesting area for yellow-eyed penguins (Megadyptes antipodes). In 2024, the last breeding-age female at Sandfly Bay, who had been consistently producing chicks for a dozen years, drowned in a fishing net. In the 2008-2009 breeding season, there were 739 breeding pairs in the mainland New Zealand population. But the population has dropped since then to 117 pairs — a decline of more than 80%. The IUCN listed the species as endangered in its last assessment, in 2020, when the mainland population was still twice what it is now. Set nets act as a vertical wall anchored in the water that catches fish by their gills or entangles them.

guard.title: Explainer: How sea level rise poses an ‘existential threat’ to humans, heritage and nature
guard.text: The world’s oceans are currently rising at a faster rate than at any time in at least the past three millennia, with human influence the dominant cause of sea level rise since at least 1970. At the UN general assembly in New York this week, world leaders are set to adopt a high-level declaration on the existential threats posed by sea level rise. On average, global sea levels rose by 20 centimetres between 1901 and 2018. Ocean levels rising 10.6cm since 1993. Under a moderate-emissions scenario, scientists predict global average sea level will rise an additional 56cm by 2100, relative to a 1995-2014 baseline. Around 770 million people — 10% of the world’s population — are at acute risk of negative impacts from sea level rise, according to a report from the UN secretary general released last month. By: Dr Giuliana Viglione.

guard.title: Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022
guard.text: An area of Amazon forest roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey has remained standing due to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s leadership of Brazil, according to Carbon Brief analysis. Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election to become president of the nation that is home to nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest. Amazon deforestation likely to hit its lowest level on record this year. Carbon Brief’s analysis suggests that at least 20,000 square kilometres of deforestation has been avoided since Lula took office. The analysis is based on modelling by an international research team of an alternative scenario in which Brazil’s flagship forest code legislation was not enforced — a proxy for Jair Bolsonaro’s leadership. Experts tell Carbon Brief that this estimate is likely conservative. the world’s fourth-largest emitter, whose emissions are largely driven by deforestation.

guard.title: Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs
guard.text: The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for loss and damage, following the devastating floods that hit the country in late August. This amounts to just 0.7% of the $2.7bn it has estimated in physical damage to infrastructure and economic losses from the flooding, according to Carbon Brief analysis. The $20m request would make Nepal the fourth-largest claimant. Developing countries have already made 176 applications to the UN fund, requesting in total $2.8bn. Yet predominantly developed nations have only pledged $0.8bn. No funding has been paid out of the fund since it was established in 2023. On 26 August, Nepal was hit by flash floods following a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayan border region. The flooding has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project.

guard.title: Revealing the Invisible Injustice of Extreme Heat
guard.text: The extreme heat scientists have warned about for decades came to Europe again this summer, killing at least 30,000 people like a silent, invisible plague. A 2024 United Nations report estimated about 175,000 annual heat-related deaths across Europe, and total deaths in European Union countries spiked above 60,000 in 2022 and 2024. The heat started earlier than ever, in late May. When it settled heavily over Bologna, Italy, in late June. Bologna photographer Michele Lapini made those differences visible, using his iPhone and a thermal sensor to document temperatures in homes, workplaces and public spaces. Piazza Maggiore was between 93 and 103 degrees Fahrenheit at 9:28 p.m. Story by Bob Berwyn, photos by Michele Lapini.

guard.title: Incoming El Niño Is so Extreme It Doesn’t Have a Scientific Name
guard.text: Daniel Swain, a weather and climate research scientist at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability, studies outlier events. Based on a recent study in Science, the current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium. Following this revelation, the U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres warned, "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up." Officials from Britain to Los Angeles are issuing advisories for residents to prepare and stock up on essentials in preparation for this historic El Niño. DANIEL SWAIN: So El Niño is a recharge oscillator, which is effectively a battery. The tropical oceans are a big heat sink. By Nina Dietz.

guard.title: A Century of Sand Debt Comes Due in Malibu
guard.text: The sand at Surfrider Beach has thinned to the point where, at high tide, the ocean reaches almost to the Pacific Coast Highway. The three distinct points that made Malibu’s Surfrider Beach have collapsed into one. What’s happening at Malibu is about human intervention — a century of dams, seawalls and paved-over rivers that have starved this coastline of the sediment that builds its beaches. But it is becoming a climate story, fast, because a coast stripped of its natural defenses is a coast with nothing left to absorb what’s coming. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect. A new study finds the world’s great surf breaks are vulnerable to climate change. By Kate Waxman.

reply.editorialJudgment: 一篇把地貌讲成因果链的解读：沙不是被浪带走，而是被一百年的坝、海墙与被渠化的河流断供；NOAA 气候预测中心的厄尔尼诺警报又把压力加在失去自然缓冲的海岸上。nov 7 来自这个反直觉的归因，act 4 来自“沉积物预算”这套可迁移判读法。
reply.titleZh: 解读：马里布的“沙债”到期——先断供的是沉积物
reply.summaryZh: 马里布 Surfrider Beach 的沙已薄到高潮时海水几乎抵到 Pacific Coast Highway，原本三处各异的起浪点合并成一处，浪形随之改变。Inside Climate News 给出的因果是人为干预——一百年的坝、海墙与被铺掉的河流，把这条海岸赖以成滩的沉积物断了供；NOAA 气候预测中心的厄尔尼诺警报，又压在一个已无缓冲可吸收来势的海岸上。

guard.title: The Trump Administration’s Critical Minerals Agenda Comes for America’s ‘Forgotten Wildlife Corridor’
guard.text: MCDERMITT CALDERA, Ore. — On a cold and overcast spring morning, Katie Fite stood in one of the country’s last sage-grouse strongholds. Millions of sage-grouse once filled the West, but federal data shows their numbers have plummeted 80 percent since 1965 as more than a million acres of the sagebrush landscape they depend on is lost every year. Now a mining company wants to extract lithium here. Fite, public lands director for WildLands Defense, asked as she walked through the mating area, known as a lek, on the public lands where the McDermitt Lithium project would dig. The project’s owner agreed to avoid drilling during the sage-grouse breeding season. But there is so little sagebrush habitat left, Fite said, that you can’t even pretend to mitigate this. This investigation was reported in a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations. By Wyatt Myskow.

reply.editorialJudgment: 调查有明确论点且有实据：联邦数据显示 sage-grouse 自 1965 年下降 80%、每年丧失逾百万英亩艾草生境，而矿方减缓措施只到“繁殖季不钻井”。它把能源转型的上游空间成本摊开，sig/nov/cred 都给到 7；reson 5 因为落点在美国公共土地。
reply.titleZh: 调查：锂矿议程开进美国“被遗忘的野生动物走廊”

guard.title: To tackle environmental crime, track profits through the whole supply chain (commentary)
guard.text: The world has spent a decade trying to put a price on nature, yet the criminal economy has been putting a price on it for much longer. Land grabbing, illegal logging, illicit gold mining and wildlife trafficking are extremely lucrative and have become a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action, a new op-ed argues. The world is still working out how much a standing forest is worth. Criminal markets settled on a price for a felled one long ago. This article is a commentary. In a new paper for the Brookings Institution, we argue that environmental crimes are a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action. They also drain revenue from legitimate companies and public coffers. responsibility falls to park rangers, customs officials and specialized police. That view badly underestimates what is happening.

guard.title: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial
guard.text: The descriptions of a super-sized, Godzilla-level El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. It may be the strongest in at least a millennium. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. The Guardian view | Editorial.

reply.editorialJudgment: 立论明确（自然现象 + 人为愚蠢 = 致命组合，落点是而不只是天气而是不公正），reson 8 靠的是它把印度季风缺口 50%、斯里兰卡饮水水库枯竭与欧洲食物供应连成一片。数字全部转述他人，cred 5、nov 5，T2 门槛 76 下必然不入选。
reply.titleZh: 社论：超级厄尔尼诺是自然现象与人为愚蠢的致命组合
reply.summaryZh: 卫报社论把本轮“Godzilla-level”厄尔尼诺读成自然现象与人为愚蠢的叠加：它可能是至少一千年来最强，太平洋升温已超过此前高点，明年几乎肯定成为有记录以来最热一年。World Food Programme 警告 5,000 万人可能被推入急性饥饿，另有估计称仅厄尔尼诺的额外高温到 2 月就会造成 45 万人死亡。落点是：这不只是天气问题，而是不公正。
